reason: This passage from Genesis 27 emphasizes strict hierarchy extensively. The narrative centers on a patriarchal blessing that explicitly establishes dominion and superiority. The blessing itself states that Jacob shall have nations serve him ('יַעַבְדוּךָ עַמִּים'), peoples bow to him ('וְיִשְׁתַּחֲווּ לְךָ לְאֻמִּים'), and that he shall be master over his brothers ('הֱוֵה גְבִיר לְאַחֶיךָ'). The entire narrative assumes a strict hierarchical system with the father (Isaac) as ultimate authority, the firstborn (Esau) having initial privilege, and clear family rankings. The deception Jacob employs demonstrates precisely how important and valued the hierarchical position is—one risks severe consequences to obtain higher status. There is no indication that hierarchy is discouraged; rather, the text reinforces its significance.
